newsitem.title: UK: Possible new asthma treatment targets molecule.
newsitem.headline: Possible new asthma treatment targets molecule.

text.p: U.S. researchers said on Wednesday they may have opened up a possible new route for treating asthma by blocking the effects of one of the most common compounds in the body -- adenosine.

A spray containing "antisense" DNA meant to block production of adenosine reduced allergic response in rabbits by 75 percent, Jonathan Nyce of EpiGenesis Pharmaceuticals and James Metzger of East Carolina University, both in Greenville, North Carolina, said.
Adenosine, one of the most common molecules in the body, is known to be involved in asthma in some way but scientists are not sure how.

Nyce's group obstructed adenosine on the genetic level, by synthesising DNA that blocked production of adenosine. This "antisense" DNA was put into an aerosol which they sprayed on rabbits conditioned to be allergic to dust mites, a known trigger of asthma.
The sprayed rabbits barely responded to either pure adenosine or to dust mites, while rabbits sprayed with an inert substance still reacted.
"These findings suggest that adenosine is an important mediator of both airway obstruction and inflammation," the researchers wrote in a report in the science journal Nature.
"It's a really good start," said Peter Richardson, a pharmacologist at Cambridge University in England.
But Richardson, who wrote a commentary on the findings, pointed out that it is still not clear how adenosine affects the human lung, especially in asthma.
"There is already evidence that adenosine can activate mast cells, and that this is probably how it elicits bronchoconstriction (closing of the airways) in asthmatic patients," he wrote.
Mast cells are a first line of defence in the body. Coated with antibodies, they send out signals to other cells when they contact an allergy-causing chemical.
But adenosine is so common that it is a hard compound to target. As adenosine triphosphate (ATP) it helps cells release their energy -- so no one would want to suppress it completely.
Richardson said the idea of using an antisense DNA was a good one. "This sort of technology is already in clinical trials for HIV and cancer," he said.
In those diseases it is hard to target the cancer cells or HIV-infected cells. As asthma affects the airways, it is easy to get the DNA to the target.
"It's just a little bit more work and then somebody will have to be brave enough to try it," Richardson said.
Asthma is one of the most common diseases in industrialised countries, where about one in 10 children and one in 20 adults suffer from it.
